etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English polishen, from Old French poliss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of polir, from Latin polīre (“to polish, make smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive, strike, thrust”), from the notion of fulling cloth.

definitions.definition: Refinement; cleanliness in performance or presentation.
(transitive) To shine; to make a surface very smooth or shiny by rubbing, cleaning, or grinding.

quote.citation: 1699, William Temple, Heads designed for an essay on conversations‎[1]:
quote.text: Study gives strength to the mind; conversation, grace: the first apt to give stiffness, the other suppleness: one gives substance and form to the statue, the other polishes it.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To apply shoe polish to shoes.
(intransitive) To become smooth, as from friction; to receive a gloss; to take a smooth and glossy surface.

quote.citation: a. 1626, Francis Bacon, Inquisitions touching the compounding of metals:
quote.text: The other [gold], whether it will polish so well Wherein for the latter [brass] it is probable it will

definitions.definition: (transitive) To refine; to wear off the rudeness, coarseness, or rusticity of; to make elegant and polite.
